# The rules a firm actually follows {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## Count the rules in a phone {.scrollable}

Walk through one product's supply chain and ask who wrote each rule it obeys. Read the right-hand column: **most were not written by a government**.

| Rule | Written by |
|---|---|
| The radio interface | 3GPP — an industry partnership |
| Wi-Fi | IEEE — a professional association |
| The charging port | a private consortium — then made mandatory by the EU |
| The factory's quality and environmental systems | ISO 9001, ISO 14001 |
| The supplier's minerals due diligence | OECD guidance, industry schemes, buyer codes |

::: {.get}
**Private authority:** non-state actors making rules others treat as binding. For a firm, a **risk** — a standard written elsewhere becomes a condition of market access — and a **lever**: shape the standard, shape the market.
:::

# The governance triangle {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## Abbott & Snidal (2009) {.scrollable}

Abbott and Snidal map rule-setting schemes in a triangle whose corners are the three types of actor that can write rules. A scheme's position shows who runs it.

```
                       STATE
                        /\
                       /  \
                      /    \
                     /      \
                    /________\
                FIRM          NGO
```

- Near a **corner**: one actor type — industry code (firms), activist label (NGOs), treaty (states)
- In the **middle**: hybrids — multi-stakeholder certification (firms and NGOs); the UN Global Compact (all three)
- **The shadow of the state**: private schemes are shaped by the threat — or promise — of public regulation, and by states choosing to endorse, require or ignore them

::: {.muted}
In W. Mattli & N. Woods (Eds.), *The Politics of Global Regulation*, Princeton UP, pp. 44–88.
:::

## Put it to the room

> Place these in the triangle: **FSC**, **UN Global Compact**, **ISO 14001**, **an industry code of conduct**, **the EU's common charger rule**.

Ask of each: who wrote it, who can change it, and who would enforce it if a firm ignored it.

::: {.warn}
The placement predicts the behaviour: who can change the scheme, who finds it legitimate, whether a state may make it mandatory.
:::

# Standards and power {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## Who wins at ISO and the IEC? Mattli & Büthe (2003) {.scrollable}

When an *international* product standard is written, whose version wins? Mattli and Büthe test three explanations against each other. Decide which you expect before the answer appears.

| Explanation | Prediction |
|---|---|
| **Technological rationality** | the best technology wins, whoever proposes it |
| **Primacy of power** | the largest markets win |
| **Institutional complementarity** | those whose **domestic** standard-setting matches the international structure win |

::: {.fragment}
::: {.get}
Their evidence favours **institutional complementarity**: coordinated European national bodies were better placed than the fragmented US system. Influence over "technical" rules depends on how a country — and its firms — are organised to take part.
:::
:::

::: {.muted}
*World Politics*, 56(1), 1–42. [doi:10.1353/wp.2004.0006](https://doi.org/10.1353/wp.2004.0006)
:::

## Technical standards are geopolitics

Each of these is a competition between blocs, each trying to make its domestic rules the world's. The firm that builds to the losing standard rebuilds.

- **Telecoms** — whose patents and specifications are in the next generation?
- **Batteries and charging** — whose formats become the default?
- **AI and data** — whose rules does a global firm adopt everywhere?

::: {.step}
**The Brussels effect** (Bradford, 2020): it is often cheaper for a firm to adopt the strictest rule everywhere than to run two product lines — which is how EU rules become global.
:::

# Three perspectives; delegated or entrepreneurial {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## Brunsson, Rasche & Seidl (2012)

Three ways to look at the same standard: what it does to the firm that adopts it, who writes it, and how it orders a whole market.

| Standardization… | Example |
|---|---|
| ***of*** organizations | ISO 14001 tells a firm how to organise environmental management |
| ***by*** organizations | the bodies that write standards, and how they work |
| ***as*** organization | standards ordering markets and fields without formal hierarchy |

::: {.warn}
Standards are **dynamic**: revised, contested, translated locally — and **decoupled**. A certificate is not a practice: a firm certified to ISO 14001 may run its plants exactly as before.
:::

## Green (2013)

Private authority has two sources, and they fail in different ways. Ask where a rule's authority comes from before deciding how durable it is.

| | **Delegated** | **Entrepreneurial** |
|---|---|---|
| **Origin** | states hand over rule-making | private actors create rules others adopt |
| **Illustration** | verification under the Clean Development Mechanism | voluntary carbon accounting, e.g. the GHG Protocol |
| **Watch** | the state can take it back | adoption — the rule is as strong as its users |

::: {.muted}
Green's field is carbon governance. For a firm, a delegated rule is a political risk — it moves with the state that delegated it; an entrepreneurial rule is a market risk — it moves with the number of firms and investors that use it.
:::

# Race to the bottom, or trading up? {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## Two scenarios

Both start from the same fact — trade intensifies competition — and predict opposite directions for standards. Which one holds is an empirical question.

::::: columns

:::: {.column width="50%"}

### Race to the bottom

Trade intensifies competition → governments and firms cut environmental standards to attract investment and win exports.

::::

:::: {.column width="50%"}

### Trading up — the California effect

Exporters to strict markets adopt strict standards → trade spreads them (Vogel, 1995).

::::

:::::

::: {.muted}
The difference lies in who sets the bar. In the first, the exporter's own government competes for investment; in the second, the customer's market decides what an exporter must meet.
:::

## Prakash & Potoski (2006) {.scrollable}

ISO 14001 makes a clean test: it is voluntary, so no law forces adoption, and any pull from export markets shows up directly in the data.

- **ISO 14001**: voluntary, beyond what many domestic laws require
- **Panel**: 108 countries, seven years
- **Key variable**: adoption in a country's **export markets**

::: {.get}
**Finding:** trade linkages **encourage** ISO 14001 adoption when a country's major export markets have adopted it. Standards travel towards the customer's — trading up, not racing to the bottom.
:::

::: {.muted}
*AJPS*, 50(2), 350–364. [doi:10.1111/j.1540-5907.2006.00188.x](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-5907.2006.00188.x)
:::

## For the firm {.scrollable}

::: {.warn}
"Voluntary" is not "optional". A standard your buyers require is as binding as a law — and it can become a condition of market access without a single law changing.
:::

- Monitor what your **customers' home markets** adopt, not only what your host government legislates
- Decide: **adopt** early, **shape** in the committee, or **resist** — each has a cost
- Remember the decoupling point: a buyer may accept the certificate, but an NGO or a regulator may look at the practice

Mattli and Büthe's lesson applies to firms as well as countries: influence goes to those organised to take part, and taking part is expensive.

> **Put it to the room:** two engineers, a quarter of their time, three years on an ISO committee. Worth it?

# The Tableau skill of the day {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## Maps and Pages {.scrollable}

The practice maps how ISO 14001 spread. Raw certificate counts mostly measure economic size, so the map shows certificates per billion US$ of GDP.

1. `iso3` → *Geographic Role* → **Country/Region** — Tableau recognises ISO 3166 codes
2. Check the **unknown** indicator at the bottom right → *Map → Edit Locations* to fix what it could not place
3. **Filled map** of certificates per billion US$ of GDP — sequential palette, never a rainbow
4. `Year` → **Pages** shelf → press play to animate the diffusion
5. **Small multiples**: `Region` × `Year`, line of the median country — the same story, without animation, on one page

::: {.check}
Never join or geocode on names. Hong Kong, Taiwan, Korea and Türkiye will tell you why.
:::
